newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia rights groups complain of persecution.
newsitem.headline: Russia rights groups complain of persecution.

text.p: Political leaders in provincial Russia are jailing local human rights campaigners on trumped-up charges as part of a generally repressive attitude to criticism, rights activists said on Thursday.

Speaking at the Moscow launch of a damning Amnesty International report accusing Russian police of widespread use of torture, campaigners cited several examples of activists being held without trial on questionable grounds.

"Alas...we must declare that political persecution has begun again in Russia, persecution of human rights activists for their human rights activities," Lyudmila Alexeyeva, head of the Moscow Helsinki lobby group, told a news conference.

Valery Abramkin, director of the Moscow Centre for Prison Reform, accused regional authorities of launching a "mass" campaign of repression against activists who dared criticise their "feudal authority" over local populations.

The weakness of the federal government and sheer size of the world's largest country give local governors, judges and police vast autonomy from Moscow. The three examples cited at the news conference were all in relatively remote regions -- Magadan in the Far East, Arkhangelsk in the Far North and Omsk in Siberia.

In all three cases over the past few months, the activists involved were released, but only through the personal intervention of liberal members of President Boris Yeltsin's Kremlin staff, rather than through normal legal channels.
"As before, it's the phone call from above that rules, not the law," Alexeyeva said.

Only on Thursday, Rafael Usmanov was ordered freed on Kremlin orders after two weeks on remand for allegedly slandering a judge in the far eastern Magadan region, site of some of the worst Soviet GULag labour camps.

Usmanov, who has faced a number of similar charges in the past two years, has campaigned against police torture and other human rights abuses and spoken up for defendants in court, the Moscow activists said.

A statement by Usmanov, distributed in Moscow, compared his treatment to that meted out to those who dared argue against public prosecutors in the show trials that marked the height of Stalin's purges of the communist party in 1937.
Written before news of his release, he said he would continue to a hunger strike to the end if necessary.
"I know my health has been undermined and continuing my hunger strike could have the most negative consequences for me. Yet I have no choice," he wrote.

Activists said it took a phone call from Anatoly Chubais, then Yeltsin's chief aide and now first deputy prime minister, to save Omsk human rights campaigner Yuri Shadrin from starving to death in police custody at the end of December.
The Amnesty International report, published in London last week, accused the Russian government of failing to stop systematic use of torture by police and prison officers.
It called on Yeltsin to repeal decrees allowing the authorities to hold suspects for 30 days without charge and to ensure all Russian officials knew that torture was a crime.

Apart from such cruelties as "The Elephant" -- fitting a gas mask and cutting off the air or filling it with tear gas -- the gross overcrowding of prisons and pre-trial detention centres amounted in itself to torture under international law, it said.
